chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from one of his companions, from Aban, from Muhammad al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

It is not permissible for a man to sell using a Sa' other than the Sa' of the people of the city, for indeed a man hires a camel driver and measures for him with the Mudd of his house; perhaps it will be smaller than the Mudd of the marketplace. And if he were to say, 'This is smaller than the Mudd of the marketplace,' he would not be bound by it, but he would bear that and place it in his trustworthiness.
And he (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not correct except for one Mudd, and the trustees are at this status.'

key_terms.أَمَانَتِهِ: His trustworthiness/trust: The concept of amanah, implying the measure used is held in trust or accounted for fairly.
key_terms.صَاع: Sa': A traditional unit of volume measurement, typically four handfuls.
key_terms.صَاعُ أَهْلِ الْمِصْرِ: Sa' of the people of the city: The standard, recognized measure used in the local market.
key_terms.مُدّ: Mudd: A traditional unit of volume measurement, typically one handful.
key_terms.مُدّ السُّوق: Mudd of the marketplace: The standard measure used in commercial trade.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on using different measurement units in Islamic trade transactions?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi underscores the Shia legal principle of 'urf' (customary practice) in commercial law, mandating that the standard measure of the local market prevails over individual or household variations to prevent hidden deception (gharar). It highlights the juristic distinction between the physical act of measuring and the moral accountability of the seller, ensuring transparency in trade. This ruling reinforces the broader Islamic ethical framework where commercial integrity is maintained through adherence to recognized local standards rather than arbitrary personal metrics.
